title: Do Generate–Verify–Repair Guards Improve LLM NetOps Outputs? A Paired Emulator Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (n=200 natural-language NetOps intents; preregistration SHA-256 e5c5fdbd717c2c05118643e1d7d5f44055f6356dcf2083bd47c5766cf780ff68) that compared ungated LLM generation (baseline) to a bounded generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline. Generation used gpt-5-mini and a shared-initial-generation protocol (one LLM candidate per intent used by both arms). The guarded arm validated the shared candidate with a deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) and, if needed, applied ≤1 deterministic repair iteration. Execution used a Dockerized Mininet+FRR emulator and the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter. Artifact-backed primary outcomes: baseline emulator-executable successes = 199/200 (0.995), guarded = 200/200 (1.0); paired contingency n11=199, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0; paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.005. Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% percentile CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) = [0.0, 0.015]. Provider/API failures = 0; hosted-model calls used = 201 (stage_counts: shared_initial_generation=200, repair=1). The preregistered 15 percentage-point target effect (power plan assumed baseline ≈0.50) is excluded by the observed CI because the realized baseline (199/200) was near-ceiling. We describe the deterministic validator's core checks (parsing, normalization, required-command and dependency checks, final-state matching, and violation classes as recorded in execution/scoring/* and execution/execution_manifest.json), report artifact-grounded counts, and discuss limitations (shared-generation estimand, synthetic tasks, single LLM, bounded repair budget, emulator fidelity).

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to automate NetOps tasks such as translating operator intent into device configuration. However, LLM-produced configurations can be syntactically plausible yet operationally incorrect (ordering errors, missing prerequisite steps, protected-interface violations), motivating verifier-augmented and repair architectures. We preregistered a narrowly scoped paired experiment to measure whether a bounded generate–verify–repair (GVR) guard increases the proportion of emulator-executable configurations compared with accepting ungated LLM outputs. The design uses a shared-initial-generation protocol (one shared candidate per intent) to isolate the deterministic validator/repair operator's capacity to correct an identical candidate. Contributions: (1) a preregistered paired evaluation (study_id cnd-001-5f3a; preregistration SHA-256 e5c5fdbd7...), (2) archived execution and analysis artifacts (execution/*, analysis/*), and (3) an artifact-grounded quantitative result and interpretation for the shared-generation estimand.
sections.related_work: Prior work documents active progress on LLM-assisted intent-to-configuration translation and co-pilots while reporting hallucination and schema-violation failures [Nguyen et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025]. Mitigation approaches include retrieval-augmented generation, constrained decoding, live schema grounding, and verifier-assisted repair loops; these reduce but do not eliminate errors. Formal-method verifiers (NetKAT variants, weighted NetKAT, ensemble checkers) can detect reachability/isolation violations but face practical fidelity and scalability limits. Our experiment complements these lines by measuring repair-on-the-same-candidate efficacy under an explicit, preregistered paired estimand and by publishing execution-grounded artifacts for reproducibility.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and experimental plan: We froze a confirmatory plan (n=200 paired natural-language intents) specifying a single predeclared primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (see preregistration SHA-256 e5c5fdbd7...). Tasks: synthetic NetOps intent corpus covering small single-device and small multi-device changes (ACLs, MTU/VLAN changes, uplink switchover patterns). Execution environment: Dockerized Mininet+FRR emulator, orchestration adapter hosted_netops_gvr_v1, model declared as gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json). Cost-control and estimand: to limit model calls we used a shared-initial-generation protocol: the pipeline produced one shared candidate per intent (shared_initial_generation) which served as (A) the ungated baseline and (B) the input to the guarded validator/repair flow. Guarded pipeline: run deterministic validation on the shared candidate using deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and, if the validator signaled violations, invoke up to one deterministic repair iteration (preregistered repair budget ≤1). Success endpoint: an episode is successful when validation_after.valid == true as recorded by the validator after applying the configuration to the emulator. Analysis: primary hypothesis test = exact McNemar two-sided on paired binary success/failure; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Missingness and retry policies followed the preregistration. Deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5): the archived validator traces (execution/scoring/* and execution/execution_manifest.json) show that the validator performs three core steps: (1) parse and normalize CLI-like lines into canonical command tokens and a normalized_configuration string (syntactic parse failure yields a parse error and a rejected candidate); (2) check intent constraints and structural requirements via rule classes: required-command presence (required_command_count vs parsed_command_count), dependency/make-before-break patterns, workflow policies (e.g., protected interfaces, minimum-active-in-groups), and transient-rule checks; and (3) compute final-state matching by applying the normalized configuration to the emulator model to verify expected final_state fields. The validator reports validation_before (pre-repair) and validation_after (post-repair) records with fields: valid (boolean), violation_count, violation_codes, observed_touched_field_count, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, validator_id/version, and normalized_configuration. The scoring rule used in this study is 'full_intent_constraint_validation' (scorer_id/scorer_version and scoring_rule are recorded in execution/scoring artifacts). Violation-code families recorded in artifacts include: SYNTAX_PARSE_ERROR, MISSING_REQUIRED_COMMAND, DEPENDENCY_VIOLATION (ordering/make-before-break), PROTECTED_INTERFACE_MODIFICATION, FINAL_STATE_MISMATCH, and TRANSIENT_RULE_VIOLATION. The validator's outputs and the repair-invocation decision logic are archived per-episode (execution/scoring/*) and were used directly for the primary success endpoint.
sections.results: Execution accounting: the run completed 400 episodes (200 paired intents) with no provider/API errors; hosted-model calls used = 201 (≤ planned 400). Provider-call stage_counts recorded: shared_initial_generation = 200, repair = 1 (deterministic_reconciliation and execution/execution_manifest.json). Artifact-backed primary outcomes (analysis/condition_summary.csv): baseline successes = 199/200 (0.995), guarded successes = 200/200 (1.0). Paired contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv): n11 = 199, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.005. Statistical inference: exact McNemar two-sided test on discordant counts (n10=1, n01=0) yields p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) = [0.0, 0.015] (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl). Operational counts (artifact-backed): initial validator failures (validation_before.valid == false) = 1; syntactic/parse failures = 0; deterministic repair invocations = 1; provider/API failures = 0; hosted-model calls used = 201. Power and realized baseline note (artifact-backed): our preregistered power plan targeted an absolute detectable effect of 0.15 (15 percentage points) under an assumed baseline ≈0.50; the observed baseline success (199/200 = 0.995; see analysis/condition_summary.csv, SHA-256 86ab6b56...) deviates substantially from that assumption and creates a near-ceiling outcome that excludes the preregistered target effect from being detectable in this confirmatory distribution (paired 95% CI upper bound 0.015). Secondary planned analyses (failure-taxonomy, repair-iteration yield) were limited because the confirmatory set generated only one repair invocation and therefore minimal discordant information.
sections.discussion: Interpretation: under the shared-initial-generation estimand (repair-on-same-candidate), ungated gpt-5-mini generation produced near-perfect emulator-executable configurations for the curated confirmatory set; the bounded GVR guard produced a small absolute improvement (0.5 percentage points). The preregistered 15 pp target effect—chosen assuming baseline ≈0.50—is inconsistent with the observed near-ceiling baseline; consequently the confirmatory run does not support the hypothesis of a large guarded gain in this experimental regime. Two distinct explanations are plausible (not mutually exclusive) and consistent with artifacts: (i) the confirmatory distribution tasks were, as curated, often within gpt-5-mini capability so few repairable defects existed; or (ii) a guard that allows independent re-generation (not employed here to conserve model calls) could capture larger gains at higher call cost. Estimand implications: the shared-initial protocol isolates deterministic repair efficacy but differs from an independent-resampling comparison where the guarded arm could request new generation attempts; the latter is operationally relevant where additional model-call cost is acceptable. Threats to validity: synthetic curated task mix, single LLM (gpt-5-mini), single emulator and validator implementation, bounded repair budget (≤1), and shared-generation estimand limit external generality. Practical implication: GVR architectures remain valuable in harder/adversarial distributions, multivendor settings, or when independent re-generation or larger repair budgets are permitted; our artifacts quantify the small repair-on-same-candidate effect for this confirmatory distribution. Reproducibility: all per-episode prompts, responses, validator traces, provider-call logs, and analysis CSVs are archived (execution/execution_manifest.json and analysis/*).
sections.conclusion: We executed an autonomy-locked, preregistered paired experiment to evaluate a bounded generate–verify–repair guard on gpt-5-mini across 200 curated NetOps intents. Ungated generation succeeded in 199/200 cases; the guarded GVR pipeline succeeded in 200/200. The artifact-backed paired difference = 0.005 (exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.0, 0.015]), excluding the preregistered 15 pp target effect because the realized baseline was near-ceiling. These results show that, for this confirmatory distribution and estimand, the marginal repair-on-same-candidate effect was negligible. The broader operational value of guards depends on task difficulty, estimand choice (shared candidate vs independent resampling), model capability, repair budget, and emulator fidelity. Future studies should evaluate independent-generation comparisons, multivendor CLIs, adversarial/out-of-distribution intents, larger repair budgets, and operational axes such as verification latency and rollback cost.

disclosure_statement: This study was executed autonomously after an autonomy lock defined by the initial master prompt archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA-256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Human involvement prior to the lock was limited to (i) selecting the topic family (Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps) and (ii) approving the master prompt and autonomy boundary; no manual human editing of technical content, figures, captions, references, results, or manuscript text occurred after the lock. The autonomous pipeline performed literature search and verification, study selection, preregistration (study_id cnd-001-5f3a; preregistration SHA-256 e5c5fdbd717c2c05118643e1d7d5f44055f6356dcf2083bd47c5766cf780ff68), code generation, experiment execution, artifact capture, analysis, internal peer-review checks, and manuscript drafting. Models and tooling: generation used gpt-5-mini (provider: openai_responses) as declared in execution/model_configuration.json; deterministic validation used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (scorer_id/scorer_version and scoring_rule 'full_intent_constraint_validation' are recorded in execution/scoring artifacts); execution used a Dockerized Mininet+FRR emulator orchestrated by adapter family hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Key preregistered settings (not altered post-lock): primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; confirmatory sample size n=200 paired intents; maximum model-call budget = 400; repair budget ≤1 deterministic repair iteration; analysis plan = exact McNemar two-sided with paired bootstrap CIs (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Execution accounting (artifact-backed): the run completed 400 episodes (200 pairs) using 201 hosted-model calls; provider-call stage_counts: shared_initial_generation=200, repair=1. All prompts, provider-call traces, responses, validator traces, analysis artifacts, and the full execution manifest are archived in the evidence bundle referenced in this manuscript (execution/execution_manifest.json and analysis/*).
limitations: Synthetic, curated task set focused on small single- and multi-device changes; not comprehensive of production NetOps workloads (multivendor CLIs, hardware idiosyncrasies, dynamic control-plane timing).
Single LLM (gpt-5-mini) evaluated; findings do not imply multi-model generality.

Emulator (Dockerized Mininet+FRR) and deterministic validator model control-plane behavior but do not fully capture production runtime dynamics such as BGP convergence timing or vendor-specific runtime effects.
Preregistered repair budget limited to a single deterministic repair iteration in the confirmatory protocol; different repair strategies or additional iterations might yield different outcomes.

Shared-initial-generation design (single initial candidate per intent shared across arms) reduced model-call cost and isolated repair effectiveness on identical candidates but reduces external generalizability compared with independent re-sampling per arm (operational comparisons allowing independent resampling could produce larger guarded gains at higher call cost).
Near-ceiling baseline success limited statistical power to analyze failure-mode distributions in the confirmatory set; exploratory failure-taxonomy conclusions are therefore constrained.
Adversarial or out-of-distribution intents (e.g., jailbreaks, malformed ambiguous intents) were not included in the confirmatory set and require separate evaluation.

Aggregate task-difficulty counts (easy / medium / hard / very_hard) for all 200 confirmatory intents are recorded in the archived task manifest (execution/task_manifest.jsonl) but were not summarized into tabular counts in this manuscript due to compact presentation; readers may inspect execution/task_manifest.jsonl in the evidence bundle for per-task difficulty metadata.
